title: Juzgar
label: ch:es-juicio
canDo: I can follow a clinic from the door to the results: which door when it is serious, what the doctor ordered, what somebody mentioned about it, and how to apologise for dropping the form.

payoff.summary: Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
payoff.note: Wordlist derived by the solo-blocker rule (ch440); four words, so six lessons rather than seven. TWO LATIN WORDS FOR PRESSING, AND THE PRESSURE RUNS OPPOSITE WAYS: la prisa already carries premere-latin, la urgencia is urgere, and 'tengo prisa' puts it on YOU while 'es urgente' puts it on the MATTER -- you can have prisa about something not urgente and vice versa. THE CHAPTER ALSO STATES THE LIMIT OF ETYMOLOGY, which is the honest counterweight to eight chapters of it paying off: analisis (ana- + lyein, loosening the knots apart) and urgencia behave as their roots suggest, but TORPE DOES NOT -- turpis meant SHAMEFUL, a heavy accusation, and torpe is now what you call yourself after knocking a glass over, nearly an apology. The repaso's line is that a root tells you where a word came from and NEVER how hard it lands today; meanings soften and harden, so etymology guides shape, not tone. Two grammar points that pay beyond the chapter: a noun ending in unstressed -is is INVARIABLE in the plural (el/los analisis, la/las crisis) because a word already ending in s without final stress takes no plural ending -- contrast los examenes, which changes AND gains an accent to hold the stress; and every -mente adverb is a fossil of mentem, feminine because mens was, which is why it is rapidamente and never rapidomente. comentar is milder than English 'comment' -- closer to mention or talk over -- and the payoff turns on both writers picking the softest option available twice each, which is why the message reads as calm.
